summary: Deep technical session to validate Quasar Systems' on-prem inference strategy. Focus: interaction between KV cache prefetch strategies (wavefront/pipeline), kernel selection heuristics, and CUDA Graph replay behavior across TRT-LLM and vLLM runtimes. Primary goals: identify stability knobs for CUDA Graph replay, quantify latency variability with prefetch wavefront, and outline pilot instrumentation for on-prem NVLink cluster.
topics: KV cache prefetching (wavefront vs eager vs demand)
Kernel selection heuristics across TRT-LLM and vLLM
CUDA Graph replay non-determinism and fallbacks
On-prem NVLink topology effects and NUMA
transcript:
[00:00:00] Ava Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining on time, we've got about an hour for a deep dive into the kernel-path and kv prefetch behavior for your onprem runs.
[00:00:10] Liam O'Neill: thanks Ava, yeah we've been seeing these weird tail spikes when we enable cuGraph replay, and sometimes the throughput drops after long runs.
[00:00:20] Jordan Patel: cool, can you summarize the repro pattern? is it correlated with prompt length or kv cache hit rate?
[00:00:28] Riya Kapoor: short answer: seems more pronounced on medium prompts (512-1024 tokens) with a ~30% kv hit rate. If we warm cache to 80% the spikes mostly go away. but warming isn't feasible for our multi-tenant traces.
[00:00:41] Jordan Patel: got it. so there are two knobs I usually look at: the wavefront prefetch window (how many future layers/positions we prefetch into KV) and the cudaGraph replay stability parameters — especially graph capture boundaries.
[00:00:55] Marco Ruiz: we saw that when we used a larger batch window with cuGraph enabled, some kernels switched to different kernels and then the graphs wouldn't replay identical sequences. that caused the replay to fail and the runtime to fall back, which then did full dynamic dispatch and slowed everything down.
[00:01:12] Jordan Patel: right, that fallback path is expensive. TRT-LLM's kernel selector is aggressive about fusing ops when shapes are homogeneous; vLLM's dynamic engine tends to pick more generic kernels but has fewer cuGraph-specific optimizations. so the interplay is: when prefetch changes memory usage or sequence length distribution, kernel selection flips and that breaks the deterministic graph replay.
[00:01:35] Ava Chen: just to clarify terminology: when we say "wavefront prefetch" we mean prefetching KV for upcoming token positions across layers so that the runtime can avoid stalls as tokens stream in, correct?
[00:01:44] Riya Kapoor: yes that's what we're running. we implemented a 4-token wavefront which reduced average latency by ~8% but increased variance.
[00:01:54] Jordan Patel: 4-token wavefront is small but can be enough to shift allocator behavior and cause different kernel paths. Also any prefetch that increases persistent memory pressure can flip quantized kernels to fallback FP kernels due to alignment/packing differences.
[00:02:08] Liam O'Neill: alignment/packing — can you expand on that? we use int8 quant for most models, and we thought quantized kernels are stable.
[00:02:16] Jordan Patel: int8 kernels rely on specific tensor layouts and contiguous strides. If prefetching forces additional tensors into the cache or changes the stride because you're concatenating KV shards differently, some optimized int8 fused kernels don't match and the runtime selects a different kernel (often a slower generic kernel). for TRT-LLM, that pattern is more brittle because the fusion heuristics assume stable shapes at capture time.
[00:02:38] Marco Ruiz: okay that matches our logs — we saw a kernel name switch from fused_gemm_8bit to gemm_fp32_generic right before the cuGraph replay error. the timings line up.
[00:02:48] Jordan Patel: exactly. one mitigation is to stabilize shapes during capture: pad or clamp batch shapes so the graph sees consistent tensors. another mitigation is to narrow the capture scope — capture only the steady-state token generation path and exclude the initial prefix handling or prefetch bursts.
[00:03:04] Riya Kapoor: when you say narrow capture scope, do you mean capturing per-token step instead of the whole sequence? that seems like it would defeat the purpose of cuGraph for throughput.
[00:03:12] Jordan Patel: it's a tradeoff. capture per-step yields less benefit but improves replay stability. An intermediate approach: capture at a chunk granularity (e.g., 16-token chunks) and replay chunk-wise. TRT-LLM has better chunked replay semantics if the chunks preserve shape homogeneity.
[00:03:26] Ava Chen: also remember the runtime can do staged fallback: try replay, if mismatch detected, fallback to a small JIT path rather than a full dynamic path — depending on configuration. Jordan, do you want to show the trace we attached earlier?
[00:03:38] Jordan Patel: yeah i'll pull up the NVTX trace. so here's an example run — i'll read out timestamps because the recording might blur visuals: [00:03:46] you see a contiguous block of captures starting at 00:03:50, capture ends at 00:03:58, replay at 00:03:59. the first two replays are fine but at 00:04:20 we see a kernel mismatch and the replay aborts.
[00:04:31] Jordan Patel: note the memory footprint increased by ~7% right before the mismatch; that's the prefetch buffer filling. also the scheduler interleaved a prefetch op which added a small stride mismatch.
[00:04:45] Liam O'Neill: hmm. can we control the prefetch stride or limit number of outstanding prefetch ops? our implementation seems to fire prefetches aggressively.
[00:04:54] Jordan Patel: yes, you can rate-limit the prefetch engine and set a cap on outstanding prefetch requests. Redwood's runtime exposes a prefetch window and a concurrency cap. For onprem builds you can tweak those values in the runtime config.
[00:05:06] Riya Kapoor: do you have a rule of thumb for prefetch window + kernel stability? like if we keep prefetch <= 2 tokens we avoid most kernel flips?
[00:05:12] Jordan Patel: empirically, for our test models (Llama-like arch with 32k context), prefetch <= 2 kept kernel paths stable in 90% of runs. but if your batch shapes vary a lot across requests, even a prefetch=1 can flip things. The important metric is shape variance at capture time.
[00:05:30] Marco Ruiz: our workloads are mixed — some interactive sessions (low batch, variable length) and some batched background scoring (stable shapes). is there a hybrid config we should use?
[00:05:40] Jordan Patel: hybrid approach: enable aggressive prefetch + cuGraph in the batched worker pool (dedicated nodes), and use dynamic dispatch with smaller prefetch on the interactive nodes. For onprem you can split those onto different NVLink islands to avoid noisy neighbor effects.
[00:05:56] Ava Chen: that ties into your infra question — Marco, can you share the NVLink island topology? are the interactive pods co-located with batch pods?
[00:06:03] Marco Ruiz: currently yes, both in same node pools. we might be able to isolate. i'll confirm.
[00:06:07] Riya Kapoor: one other item — quantization. we saw that quantized kernels sometimes had precision regressions after prefetch-induced kernel changes. is that expected?
[00:06:16] Jordan Patel: precision regressions usually stem from fallback to FP kernels or different accumulation kernels. it's not inherently prefetch, but the shape/kind switch causes a different math path. TRT-LLM fused int8 kernels do requantize internally; if you slip into a slower kernel it might use a different accumulation width and rounding, which shows as small distribution shifts. Those can trigger downstream eval alerts.
[00:06:36] Liam O'Neill: that explains alerts our QA flagged. ok. what about vLLM behavior? you mentioned it's more generic but less cuGraph-optimized.
[00:06:45] Jordan Patel: vLLM's scheduler is conservative: it prioritizes correctness and dynamic shapes and therefore tends to avoid highly fused int8 kernels unless shapes are perfectly stable. That means you'll see more consistent latency but less throughput in the best-case scenarios compared to TRT-LLM. Also vLLM's graph-like capture isn't as reliant on cuGraph primitives, so replay is less brittle but you lose the extra fused-kernel gains.
[00:07:07] Riya Kapoor: so TRT-LLM gives us higher peak throughput but with more fragility on our mixed workload, vLLM gives steadier tails but lower peak?
[00:07:15] Jordan Patel: succinctly yes. But there's nuance: TRT-LLM + careful capture + chunking + stable prefetch can yield both high throughput and acceptable tails. The question is operational complexity you want to take on for your onprem team.
[00:07:29] Ava Chen: we also saw mention of NUMA and multi-node NVLink effects. Jordan, quick note on NUMA: prefetch can create traffic across NUMA domains during capture and replay which increases variance.
[00:07:39] Jordan Patel: good point — if KV buffers live on a GPU that's across an NVLink hop, the prefetch increases cross-link bandwidth and can delay kernel launches on the local GPU. We recommend aligning capture to local NVLink islands and ensure your allocator pins KV shards to the local GPU where possible. For multi-node NVLink, it's critical to verify your NVSwitch topology and ensure the fastest interconnect is used for high-KV-hit paths.
[00:08:03] Marco Ruiz: our cluster is 4 nodes with mixed NVSwitch and NVLink connections. i'll map and share.
[00:08:08] Liam O'Neill: from an ops standpoint, what's the instrumentation we should add for the pilot to catch these kernel flips quickly?
[00:08:15] Jordan Patel: NVTX ranges per major runtime phase (capture, replay, prefetch dispatch), plus kernel name logging, and a lightweight continuous kernel histogram that samples kernel names over time per GPU. Also record memory footprint deltas at capture boundaries. Redwood's onprem agent can emit those and we can provide dashboards.
[00:08:33] Riya Kapoor: could you include an example of the kernel histogram format? our logging team prefers json-lines.
[00:08:39] Jordan Patel: sure — something like {timestamp, gpu_id, kernel_name, duration_us, call_site_tag}. we'll provide a collector snippet.
[00:08:49] Ava Chen: I want to highlight a recommended pilot configuration: 1) isolate batch vs interactive nodes; 2) set prefetch window=2 on interactive, 4-6 on batch with capped outstanding prefetch=3; 3) chunked cuGraph capture at 16 tokens for TRT-LLM; 4) enable kernel histogram and NVTX. we'll put that in the follow-up doc.
[00:09:09] Sofia Morales: from product, what are the risk/benefit tradeoffs for users? we need to position it for our customers.
[00:09:15] Jordan Patel: benefit is up to 2-3x throughput improvement on steady batched workloads with TRT-LLM + int8 and chunked capture. risk is operational complexity: more tuning, more brittle if workload is highly variable. vLLM gives more predictable tails but lower peak. So choose by SLA: if you must guarantee sub-100ms tails for interactive, prefer vLLM or conservative TRT config; if you optimize for cost-per-token on scoring pipelines, go TRT-LLM with the aggressive stack.
[00:09:44] Marco Ruiz: for the pilot can we try both runtimes side-by-side on similar hardware and run an A/B with real traffic?
[00:09:51] Ava Chen: yes that's the plan — we suggest a two-week A/B with instrumentation. Jordan will produce the runbook.
[00:09:58] Jordan Patel: quick note on cuGraph replay knobs: enable strict_capture_mode=false if you have small shape variance — it allows some flexibility. if you need determinism, set strict_capture_mode=true and then aggressively pad shapes. There is also a replay_tolerances table that can permit small stride changes without aborting. we'll share exact flags.
[00:10:18] Riya Kapoor: do you have any automated heuristic to switch between runtimes based on realtime metrics?
[00:10:24] Jordan Patel: Redwood runtime supports routing policies: you can route by route-model pair to a runtime group. In practice we run canaries for a set of keys and if tail-latency or kernel-failure rate exceeds thresholds, route all interactive traffic to the conservative pool while batch keeps using the aggressive pool. This is in the rollout docs.
[00:10:41] Liam O'Neill: what's the expected overhead of the routing switch? near zero?
[00:10:45] Jordan Patel: low — it's a lightweight metadata switch. Sessions that already started will finish on the existing runtime, new sessions will land on the other group. there is some session warm-up cost but it's manageable.
[00:10:57] Ava Chen: okay we're approaching the final 30 minutes mark. Jordan, can you summarize the immediate mitigations we want Quasar to try before the pilot?
[00:11:06] Jordan Patel: sure: 1) tighten prefetch concurrency cap to 2 and try wavefront=1-2 for interactive; 2) enable chunked cuGraph capture at 8-16 tokens rather than whole sequence; 3) add NVTX + kernel histogram logging; 4) pad shapes for chatty endpoints during capture; 5) run a short local bench with induced kv hit variance to validate.
[00:11:27] Riya Kapoor: we'll run the local bench tomorrow. any recommended bench scripts?
[00:11:31] Jordan Patel: we'll share a bench harness that can sweep prompt lengths, kv hit rates, prefetch values, and record kernel histograms — expect the artifact in your inbox by EOD 2029-01-20.
[00:11:41] Sofia Morales: for the pilot scope, confirm hardware requirements and expected duration?
[00:11:45] Ava Chen: we'll propose a 2-week pilot using 2 NVLink nodes for batch and 2 isolated nodes for interactive, with the instrumentation turned on. Redwood SE will run the A/B and analysis. We'll include bandwidth expectations and OS/kernel compatibility notes in the doc.
[00:11:58] Marco Ruiz: timeline works for us.
[00:12:01] Liam O'Neill: two quick clarifying Qs: 1) what about memory fragmentation over long runs? we've seen slow drift in free memory. 2) any recommended GC/allocator settings?
[00:12:11] Jordan Patel: memory fragmentation is real with aggressive prefetch + long-lived KV caches. Two mitigations: periodic draining/restart of worker after N requests, or use a compacting allocator if available (some runtimes support a defragmentation pass during low traffic). For allocator flags, set conservative growth caps and prefer pooled allocators with pre-reserved arenas for KV to avoid fragmentation into general heap. We'll include recommended flags per runtime.
[00:12:37] Riya Kapoor: great. one last item — security/compliance: since it's onprem, we need to ensure no telemetry leaks model artifacts. what's Redwood's stance?
[00:12:45] Ava Chen: for onprem we ship a control-plane agent that only ships telemetry metrics and NVTX/kernels; model weights and KV never leave the customer's network unless explicitly permitted. We'll include the security brief (SOC/ISO statements) in the follow-up.
[00:12:57] Sofia Morales: perfect.
[00:12:59] Jordan Patel: i'll summarize the technical notes in the doc: kernel flip signatures, example NVTX slices, and a list of cuGraph flags. plus the bench harness.
[00:13:10] Ava Chen: great. let's do a quick recap of action items and owners — we'll put these in the calendar invite too.
[00:13:16] Riya Kapoor: thanks everyone.
[00:13:18] Marco Ruiz: thanks.
[00:13:19] Liam O'Neill: thanks.
[00:13:20] Ava Chen: end call.
